fixtures.basis: Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement applies the state's table: its Commercial CIRC FAQ sends applicants to Table 1004.1.2 of the NC Building Code and Section 403 and Table 403.1 of the NC Plumbing Code. The county's published Plumbing Interpretations (19 pages) touch toilet counts only for parks (people counted from parking spaces, 50% male and 50% female), salons (people counted per station) and the shell phase of a building (counts reviewed at upfit); its Commercial Building interpretations add one on libraries. None changes the counts for offices, restaurants or schools, so the state pack's examples stand.
fixtures.quote: How are plumbing fixture requirements calculated for a project? The first step is to determine Occupancy load of the space using Table 1004.1.2 in the NC Building code. Once this is established, review Section 403 of the NC Plumbing Code along with table 403.1 to determine your minimum fixture count.

interpretations.quote: Subject: Park Fixture Requirements [...] Automobile parking area spaces shall be used to determine the toilet requirements for Park and Recreation areas. The total number of persons shall be figured on the basis of two (2) persons per parking space and sixty (60) persons per bus parking space. The division of facilities shall be based on 50% male / 50% female.

Subject: Occupant Load for Salons (Beauty and Nail). Effective Date: 1/1/2017 [...] The occupant load shall be calculated by the greater of the following methods: 1. Standard occupant calculation per section 1004 NCBC 2. Count each station and multiple by 1.25 (one customer per station and 1 employee per 4 stations) plus lobby/waiting areas at 1/15 occupant/sq ft

permit.exempt_list_quote: (c) No permit issued under Article 9 of Chapter 143 of the General Statutes is required for any construction, installation, repair, replacement, or alteration costing forty thousand dollars ($40,000) or less and performed in accordance with the current edition of the North Carolina State Building Code in any single-family residence, farm building, or commercial building unless the work involves any of the following: (1) The addition, repair, or replacement of load-bearing structures. However, no permit is required for replacement of windows, doors, exterior siding, or the pickets, railings, stair treads, and decking of porches and exterior decks that otherwise meet the requirements of this subsection. (2) The addition or change in the design of plumbing. However, no permit is required for replacements otherwise meeting the requirements of this subsection that do not change size or capacity. (3) The addition, replacement, or change in the design of heating, air-conditioning, or electrical wiring, devices, appliances, or equipment, other than like-kind replacement of electrical devices and lighting fixtures. (4) The use of materials not permitted by the North Carolina State Building Code. (5) The addition of roofing, excluding replacement. (6) Any changes to which the North Carolina Fire Code applies.
permit.county_quote: Appropriate permits are required for Commercial Work related to any new construction, reconstruction, alteration, repair, movement to another site, removal or demolition of any building. Permits are also required for the installation, extension, alteration or general repair of electrical, mechanical or plumbing systems. [...] However, permits may not be required for any projects with work costing $40,000 or less, unless the work involves: The addition, repair, or replacement of load bearing structures; The addition or change in the design of a plumbing system; The addition, replacement or change in the design of a heating or air conditioning system; The addition, replacement or change in the design of an electrical system; The use of materials not permitted by the code; The addition of roofing, excluding replacement of like grade fire resistance material
permit.note: The exemption is state law (G.S. 160D-1110(c)), which Mecklenburg County restates on its Permitting page. Neither names toilet partitions or compartments. On the county page the $40,000 sentence follows the paragraph on residential work, while the statute covers 'any single-family residence, farm building, or commercial building'. The statute's item (6), 'Any changes to which the North Carolina Fire Code applies', is not in the county's list. Whether a partition replacement touches the fire code (interior finish) or is 'in accordance with' the building code without a permit is not stated. The county's Small Commercial Plan Review lists 'Bathroom additions and renovations up to 1,000 sq. ft.' among the projects it reviews.
permit.second_quote: Office or bathroom renovations in occupancies other than B and M. [...] Bathroom additions and renovations up to 1,000 sq. ft.
permit.office: Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement, Code Information & Resource Center (CIRC)

restrooms_city.note: No Charlotte or Mecklenburg County rule on single-user restroom signs or shared all-gender rooms was found (one web search; the county enforces the state codes without local amendments, and G.S. 143-761, quoted from the state pack, bars cities and counties from regulating access to multi-stall restrooms). News reports say Charlotte's 2021 nondiscrimination ordinance doesn't mention restrooms; the City Code itself was not read (charlottenc.gov returned 'access denied'), so this is 'none found', not 'none exists'.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Charlotte job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see the Mecklenburg County rules that apply.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Charlotte office towers, schools, hospitals and distribution centers, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** North Carolina's plumbing rules set the number of toilets by how many people use the building. Mecklenburg County enforces them in Charlotte and applies them unchanged. The table below shows what that means.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Mecklenburg County issues building permits in Charlotte. Under North Carolina law, work in a commercial building that costs $40,000 or less needs no permit unless it involves load-bearing structure, a change to the plumbing, heating, air conditioning or electrical systems, materials the building rules don't allow, new roofing or anything the fire rules cover. The list doesn't name toilet partitions, and the county's plan review for small commercial projects covers bathroom renovations. Ask Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement (980-314-2633) whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.install_rule: Commercial permits in Charlotte come from Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement, and the contractor must hold the state license the work requires. North Carolina requires a state general contractor license when the project is valued at $40,000 or more, so smaller partition jobs generally don't need one. Confirm with the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: On a project valued at $40,000 or more, the contractor needs a North Carolina general contractor license.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** North Carolina has no state law setting wages on public construction, so a required wage applies only on federally funded or assisted projects over $2,000. For a carpenter on building work in Mecklenburg County that rate is $23.73 an hour plus $5.42 in benefits.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 8.25% in Charlotte: 4.75% state, 2% Mecklenburg County, 0.5% transit and a further 1% county tax that began on July 1, 2026.
page.buyers_extra: - **Office towers and corporate campuses:** one finish and one hardware standard repeated on every floor, with extra-privacy stalls where tenants ask for them.

The 2024 North Carolina State Building Code is adopted but not yet in force.

page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** North Carolina's rules call for separate men's and women's restrooms, with signs, once a space holds more than 25 people (30 for an office, 100 for a store). Where each side needs only one toilet, two single-user rooms open to anyone may be used instead, and a family restroom doesn't have to be marked for one sex. The rules in force don't provide for a shared all-gender room with several stalls, so ask Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement before planning one. State law leaves the question of who may use a multi-stall restroom to the General Assembly: state agencies, cities, counties and school boards may not set their own rules.
